rawFindings.detail: The 'postmortem' example format is reused in ~18 chapters with an identical beat-structure: open AFTER an event that 'is already over / has already failed / failed before anyone argued', state 'the trace is plain', then 'locate the one/decisive misstep' (recurring phrase) and end on a moralizing whyItMatters about finding 'the first leak, not just the final typo'. Only the noun changes (launch review, launch note, dismissal rule, product launch, TV taping, sponsor dinner, fundraiser, watercolor night, emergency memo). A reader moving chapter to chapter meets the same failed-event autopsy repeatedly. The phrases 'decisive misstep' and 'first leak' recur verbatim.

rawFindings.detail: The 'planning_choice' format recurs in ~13 chapters, and several instances match the prompt's exact second example ('protagonist has ~40 min before a board/supplier review and must choose slides vs body'). The frozen frame: protagonist has 'forty minutes / 40 open minutes / 45 minutes / 90 minutes / thirty minutes' of scarce attention before an event (board call, supplier review, meeting, parent night), nothing has started ('Nothing begins yet' / 'No work begins yet' / 'No action has started' / 'stays on paper'), and they 'budget/allocate/divide' the time into three named slots. CH23 Severin ('forty minutes before the board call... all of it on slides... budgets ten for a walk') and CH25 Weston ('40 open minutes before the supplier review... polish slides or... a quiet walk') are an almost line-for-line collision of the slides-vs-walk choice the prompt cites. The 'has N minutes before X / blank calendar / budgets the minutes / no execution yet' template is unmistakable copy-paste.

By the second domain (body, walking, solitude, sleep, hobby) this is the book's single recycled tactic dressed in new rooms, and a chapter-to-chapter reader will recognize it as copy-paste.

rawFindings.quote: CH12 ifThen: "[A mild comment lands in your body like shame.] -> If a mild comment feels like shame, then run the Soul Alignment Check and write the old meaning before you answer the present person." | CH14 ifThen: "[A mild comment lands like an attack.] -> If a mild comment lands like an attack, then Name the Old Threat by writing the exact sentence and the older meaning before you answer."
rawFindings.detail: Two chapters open their plan ifThen list with the same trigger ('a mild comment lands like shame/an attack') and the same remedy ('write the old meaning/exact sentence before you answer the present person'). CH14's quiz-opener ('You hear mild criticism and answer as if the room is attacking you') restates it again. Near-identical ifThen unit reused as the first plan branch in adjacent chapters.

rawFindings.quote: CH10 ex2: "he writes two columns on a yellow pad: mine, not mine" + MEMORABLE "The energy that was going into supervision of the universe returns to the work in front of him." | CH18 ex2/DEEP-READ: "Tamar draws three lines: accept... change... ask wisdom" + MEMORABLE "Stillness grows where the self no longer has to supervise the whole sky."
rawFindings.detail: The Stoic 'control distinction' two-column 'mine / not mine' sorting exercise is the core mechanic of both Let Go (Epictetus) and Accept a Higher Power (serenity prayer), and both close on the same 'stop supervising the universe/whole sky' image. The remedy artifact (draw columns, sort what you control) plus the supervision-of-the-sky line is effectively one reused unit split across two chapters.

rawFindings.quote: CH3 card: "choosing ahead of time what gets in and when" referenced again in CH9 "Input discipline limits the applause, outrage, gossip" | CH24 card "Earlier concept, Limit Your Inputs" | CH30 card "Earlier concept: how does input discipline support the bedtime line?" | CH33 card "Earlier concept, Limit Your Inputs: how does less noise prepare quiet courage?"
rawFindings.detail: The 'Earlier concept: Limit Your Inputs / input discipline' spaced-recall card is reused as a near-boilerplate callback in many later chapters (CH9, CH24, CH30, CH33, and others), each re-summarizing input discipline in similar phrasing. The spaced-recall convention itself is allowed, but the input-discipline recap card specifically recurs with such uniform wording that it functions as a pasted callback unit; flagged low because the surrounding question is tailored.

rawFindings.quote: CH2: "Nadia lays three cards on her kitchen table before a community board meeting" | CH5: "Make tomorrow at 9:10 a.m. a 15-minute question review at your kitchen table" | CH6: "You are alone at the kitchen table, and your first line says, 'I am failing at everything.'" | CH10: "Joshua begins his 7:00 a.m. forecast at the kitchen table" | CH11: "Put a 12-minute service check on tomorrow's calendar for 8:20 at your kitchen table" | CH14: "Put a 12-minute old-threat check on tomorrow's calendar for 8:10 a.m. at your kitchen table" | CH18: "Rosaire reads Reinhold Niebuhr's serenity prayer at the kitchen table" | CH20: "Before the change, Brandon wrote replies at the kitchen table the moment a relative mocked his budget" | CH24: "Jordan lines up four index cards beside a chipped mug at the community kitchen table" | CH26: "Put a 12-minute reset on tomorrow's calendar for 8:15 a.m. at your kitchen table" | CH29: "Place a 20-minute Being Block on tomorrow's calendar for 7:40 p.m. at your kitchen table" | CH32: "Maxime has forty minutes at the kitchen table before the house gets noisy" / "Put a 12-minute Aftermath Check on tomorrow's calendar for 8:30 p.m. at your kitchen table" | CH34: "Lorraine lays next week's calendar, a medical bill, and a Daily Stoic memento mori coin on the kitchen table"
rawFindings.detail: The 'kitchen table' is the single most stamped venue in the book, appearing in 14 of 34 chapters. It does double duty as a stamp: (1) it is the default scene setting for scenarios (CH2 Nadia's cards, CH10 Joshua's forecast, CH18 Rosaire's prayer, CH20 Brandon's budget replies, CH24 Jordan's index cards, CH32 Maxime's budget page, CH34 Lorraine's calendar) and (2) it is the venue baked into a near-identical templated TRY-NOW calendar opener that recurs almost verbatim — 'Put/Make a [N]-minute [check/reset/block] on tomorrow's calendar for [8:1x a.m.] at your kitchen table, triggered by [first inbox/criticism/quiet block]' (CH5, CH11, CH14, CH26, CH29, CH32). A paying reader moving chapter-to-chapter sees the same table, the same morning time band, and the same 'on tomorrow's calendar at your kitchen table' formula over and over, which reads as copy-paste rather than as a deliberate motif since the underlying lessons (presence, service, anger, routine, rest, mortality) are entirely different.

rawFindings.quote: CH7: "Isidore predicts the product review will sag if he borrows four minutes and thirty-three seconds..." (conference room) | CH8: "Sharon tells Constance in the empty conference room" / domain="conference room coaching" | CH16: "Adam reviews three years of compensation records at the conference room table" | CH17: "The conference room was empty except for a closed laptop and Anne Frank's chestnut tree on the screen" | CH20: "At the conference room table, Bryce brings a printed complaint to his peer mentor"
rawFindings.detail: The generic 'conference room' / 'conference room table' is stamped as the venue across 5 chapters for the workplace-review and coaching scenarios, twice with the identical 'empty conference room' framing (CH8 Sharon-Constance, CH17 HOOK). It is a low-distinctiveness corporate backdrop reused for structurally similar review/coaching beats, so a reader notices the same neutral meeting room recurring.

rawFindings.quote: CH2: "he sits in the break room for five minutes, remembers Blaise Pascal in 1654 France" | CH10: "Gregoire is midway through a donor call in the break room when he hears his own voice harden" | CH17: domain="hospital break room; audience=shift workers and caregivers" | CH20: "Hailey sends her version from the break room before the coffee cools"
rawFindings.detail: The 'break room' is reused as the venue in 4 chapters (CH2 Felix's quiet-room test, CH10 Gregoire's donor call, CH17 Malvina's nurse reset, CH20 Hailey's hot reply). Combined with the kitchen-table and conference-room stamps, the book's example settings cluster heavily into a small pool of generic office/home rooms, which compounds the copy-paste feel chapter-to-chapter.

rawFindings.quote: CH26: "The model is Benjamin Franklin's morning question and evening review, not a harsher calendar." / "What did Benjamin Franklin's morning question and evening review put on trial?" | CH29: "audience=Benjamin, a consultant who turns every break into prep" / "Benjamin writes the memo at 6:12 p.m.: 'Decision before Friday dinner: laptop closed...'" / "The closed laptop on Benjamin's desk does more than end work."
rawFindings.detail: The name 'Benjamin' is used as two different people only three chapters apart. In CH26 (Build a Routine) Benjamin Franklin is the historical source exemplar cited throughout the chapter as the model of daily routine. In CH29 (Be a Human Being) 'Benjamin' is a present-day consultant protagonist who writes a Sabbath memo. A reader who has just spent CH26 learning 'Benjamin = Benjamin Franklin, the routine guy' meets an unrelated character named simply Benjamin in CH29, creating a name collision between a famed source figure and a fictional protagonist in nearby chapters.

rawFindings.quote: CH2: "Felix tries Pascal's quiet room test twice... remembers Blaise Pascal in 1654 France" / "What does Pascal's quiet room reveal about restlessness?" | CH30: "Pascal expects the training score to jump after Madeline adds a 9 p.m. study block." / "Pascal removes the late block and moves one hard review item to the start of the workday"
rawFindings.detail: The name 'Pascal' is used as two different people. In CH2 (Become Present) 'Pascal' refers to Blaise Pascal, the 17th-century philosopher whose 'quiet room' is the chapter's source case (cited repeatedly in scenarios, cards, and quiz openers). In CH30 (Go to Sleep) 'Pascal' is an ordinary contemporary training supervisor protagonist. The same first name carries a famous philosopher in one chapter and a generic modern character in another, which a reader can register as the source-figure name being recycled onto an unrelated person.

families.name: postmortem-autopsy / failed-event trace
families.signature: Example opens AFTER an event that 'is already over / has already failed / failed before anyone argued'; narration says 'the trace is plain'; locates 'the one/decisive misstep'; whyItMatters moralizes about finding 'the first leak, not just the final typo.' Only the failed noun changes (launch review, sponsor dinner, fundraiser, emergency memo).
exemplarQuotes: CH3 [ex5]: 'Aanya's launch note failed before anyone argued. The audit found the first misstep... Postmortems help when they find the first leak, not just the final typo.'
CH10 [ex4]: 'Costa's launch postmortem begins after the angry comments have already peaked. The trace is plain... The decisive misstep was treating public status as his property.'
CH24 [ex2]: 'Anatole's fundraiser is over... The postmortem marks one decisive misstep... A postmortem is useful only when it finds the first leak.'
CH33 [ex3]: 'Zachary's emergency memo has already failed... The postmortem finds the break... He published names before the review had evidence.'
families.fix: Cap the 'postmortem' format at ~3 chapters across the book. For the other ~15, replace with a forward-looking or in-progress frame (the decision being made live, a near-miss caught, a success traced). Ban the recurring lexemes 'the trace is plain', 'decisive misstep', and 'first leak / final typo' from any future example; allow at most one chapter to use the postmortem-with-first-leak payoff and rewrite the rest.

families.name: mistake-recovery / 'halfway through, hears themselves'
families.signature: Protagonist is 'halfway through / midway through' a task (meeting, call, slide, email, testimony) when they 'hear themselves / hear their own voice' commit an error, notice it mid-stream, and correct before finishing; whyItMatters says the value is 'the noticing.' The clause 'halfway through ... hears himself/herself' is near-verbatim.
exemplarQuotes: CH1 [ex4]: 'Sierra is halfway through slide twelve when she hears herself call every initiative urgent... Sierra notices her own error before the next sentence.'
CH10 [ex5]: 'Gregoire is midway through a donor call in the break room when he hears his own voice harden.'
CH22 [ex1]: 'Lawrence is halfway through a rehab clinic meeting when he hears himself praising Stoicism...'
CH26 [ex5]: 'Minh is halfway through the wellness kickoff when he hears himself make Fred Rogers's 143 pounds sound like a medal.'
families.fix: Retire the 'halfway through X, hears himself/herself' opener. Keep at most 2 mid-stream-catch examples book-wide and vary the trigger (a colleague's glance, re-reading a sent line, a transcript). Ban the verbatim frame 'halfway/midway through ... hears [pronoun]' and the 'the value is the noticing' payoff sentence from repeating.

families.name: records-audit / 'nothing dramatic happens, the telling detail'
families.signature: Protagonist reviews/audits N weeks/months/files of records (notes, logs, clips, sheets, invoices); narration explicitly states 'Nothing dramatic happens / Nothing new happens in the room'; 'the telling detail' is one small recurring mark or blank line. This is verbatim the prompt's own first example frame.
exemplarQuotes: CH4 [ex5]: 'Ludovic studies three files at his desk... Nothing new happens in the room; the screen just changes columns. The telling detail is a copied note: too noisy to think.'
CH18 [ex3]: 'Stella audits twelve months of recovery notes in a quiet library carrel. Nothing dramatic happens except understanding... the margin phrase keeps returning: I can handle this alone.'
CH29 [ex6]: 'Soraya reviews four weeks of calendar exports, message logs, and invoices. Nothing dramatic happens. The telling detail is smaller...'
CH32 [ex1]: 'Gwen reviews six weeks of help-desk notes... The telling detail is not the word recovery; it is the blank line...'
families.fix: Because this matches the prompt's seed example, it propagated everywhere — remove that example from the authoring prompt or mark it as DO-NOT-REPRODUCE. Cap the audit format at ~3 chapters; ban the verbatim phrases 'reviews [N] [units]', 'Nothing dramatic happens / Nothing new happens in the room', and 'the telling detail.' For the rest, change the discovery vehicle (a conversation, a single live document, a comparison against a peer) rather than a records sweep.

families.name: two-person contrast / 'same X, two minds'
families.signature: Two named people '[receive/face/take/inherit] the same [X]'; one handles it badly (sends in heat / protects image / adds the luxury / keeps the phone in hand), one handles it well; diverging outcomes close on a 'same pressure, two minds' moral. The opening clause 'Name1 and Name2 [receive/face/inherit] the same...' is reused almost word-for-word.
exemplarQuotes: CH4 [ex1]: 'Hermine and Fatima face the same 40-message clinic thread... Hermine treats each line as a command... Fatima lets the heat pass...'
CH20 [ex1]: 'Nancy and Hailey receive the same forwarded complaint... Nancy drafts a reply... leaves it through lunch... Hailey sends her version from the break room before the coffee cools.'
CH24 [ex5]: 'Zoe and Lane receive the same investor request... Zoe removes two shiny features... Lane accepts both...'
CH33 [ex6]: 'Marshall and Willow receive the same draft statement... Marshall waits for his fear to clear... Willow adds two facts and signs.'
families.fix: Cap the paired-contrast format at ~3 chapters. Ban the boilerplate opener 'Name1 and Name2 [receive/face/inherit/take] the same X.' Where a contrast is genuinely the best teaching device, vary it structurally (one person across two days; a single person's two drafts; a team vs an individual) and drop the 'two minds, same pressure' tagline.

families.name: routine-reset / 'the routine breaks, stops, restarts'
families.signature: A morning/bedtime/work routine 'breaks' or 'splits' on an interruption (phone ping, alert, child, delivery, executive); protagonist physically stops (shuts lid / sets phone face down / closes inbox / hand stops on the mouse) and 'restarts' from a cleaner first move — the same three-beat machine (break > stop > restart) each time.
exemplarQuotes: CH1 [ex1]: 'Caleb begins the morning by clearing the city logistics alert wall... He catches himself racing the queue... Caleb stops, closes the alert stack, reopens the route map...'

CH3 [ex3]: 'Mateus pours coffee, opens the draft, and hears cell phone alarms... His routine has already split... Mateus closes the tabs, sets the phone face down, waits for one slow count of ten, and restarts...'
CH21 [ex5]: 'Magloire is weighing dough at 5:40 a.m. when the flour delivery fails... He sets the phone down... and restarts: one minute for the shared chain, then the call.'
CH30 [ex6]: 'Madeline's nightly routine is tea, dishwasher... She stops, puts the phone face down... and begins the tea again from the sink.'
families.fix: Cap the break/stop/restart reset at ~3 chapters and merge enforcement with the 'phone face down' remedy family (below). Ban the three-beat 'routine breaks ... stops ... restarts' machine and the stock gesture 'sets/puts the phone face down' from recurring. Vary the recovery action (name one fact aloud, step outside, ask a single question) and avoid always making the trigger a device ping.

families.name: before/after diptych / 'same object, one variable flips'
families.signature: A literal 'Before: ... After: ...' (or 'Before the change ... After the change') two-panel construction holding the SAME object/room/routine constant while one variable flips, capped by a stock line 'the X did not change' / 'the same X' / 'the facts stay the same.'
exemplarQuotes: CH2 [ex2]: 'Before: he sits in the break room for five minutes... checks headlines after forty seconds. After: he sits in the same chair, names the cup, the table edge... The room did not change; his grip on the room did.'
CH18 [ex2]: 'Before the change, Tamar refreshes the medical portal... After the change, Tamar draws three lines... The facts on the screen stay the same; the job on the page changes.'
CH22 [ex6]: 'Before the change, Lawrence's locker room routine starts with coffee, messages... After the change, the same locker holds a water bottle, walking shoes...'
CH34 [ex2]: 'Before: Douglas keeps the Daily Stoic memento mori coin in a drawer... After: the same coin sits beside the keyboard...'
families.fix: Cap the explicit Before:/After: diptych at ~3 chapters. Ban the verbatim 'Before:/After:' and 'Before the change/After the change' scaffolding and the closing tag 'the X did not change / the same X / the facts stay the same.' Where contrast-over-time is needed, narrate it as a single continuous scene rather than a two-panel template.

families.name: decision-memo / 'Subject: ... [Figure] did ... I recommend'
families.signature: A timestamped memo (7:12 p.m./4:52 p.m./11:18 p.m. etc.) opens with a 'Subject:' line whose first sentence name-drops the chapter's historical figure, followed by a one-line recommendation/refusal, capped by a whyItMatters that begins 'A written artifact/decision/order/no/choice can...'
exemplarQuotes: CH1 [ex5]: 'Tessa's memo, sent at 7:12 p.m., carries the scene: Subject: The River First. Abraham Lincoln did not stare at Vicksburg in 1863... A written artifact can protect attention after the sender closes the laptop.'
CH10 [ex6]: 'Dawson's Friday memo, 4:40 p.m., subject: Expansion recommendation. Paragraph one cites Epictetus... A written artifact can hold the boundary better than a mood can.'
CH24 [ex4]: 'Benoit writes the Friday memo... Steve Jobs made Apple focus by cutting good product strategy ideas... A written no can lower the drama.'
CH33 [ex5]: 'Antonio's memo opens: Subject: Temporary quarantine of Ward C transfers. The next line cites John F. Kennedy, October 1962...'
families.fix: Cap the timestamped 'Subject:' memo artifact at ~3 chapters. Ban the recurring 'A written [artifact/decision/order/no/choice] can...' payoff sentence and the 'Subject: line + figure name-drop + one-line recommendation' shape. Replace most with a different artifact (a spoken sentence held to, a checklist, a calendar entry) and stop pinning every memo to a precise p.m. timestamp.

families.name: planning-choice / 'N minutes before X, nothing started yet'
families.signature: Protagonist has scarce time ('forty minutes / 40 open minutes / 45 / 90 / thirty minutes') before an event (board call, supplier review, parent night); nothing has started ('Nothing begins yet' / 'No work begins yet' / 'No action has started' / 'stays on paper'); they 'budget/allocate/divide' the time into three named slots. Matches the prompt's second seed example; CH23 (slides vs walk) and CH25 (slides vs walk) are a near line-for-line collision.
exemplarQuotes: CH23 [ex2]: 'Severin has forty minutes before the board call and a blank calendar square... He budgets ten minutes for a walk, ten for one hard slide, five for water... No work begins yet; the choice is the work.'
CH25 [ex4]: 'Weston has 40 open minutes before the supplier review locks. The calendar offers three claims on that space: polish slides, answer small messages, or reserve a quiet walk...'
CH14 [ex1]: 'Amelia's parent-night agenda has 45 minutes and six hungry topics... Before any parent enters, she has to allot attention...'

CH2 [ex5]: 'Nadia lays three cards on her kitchen table... She has thirty minutes of attention to allocate... Ten for visible facts, ten for dissent, ten for the next clean step. Nothing begins yet...'
families.fix: Remove or mark DO-NOT-REPRODUCE the planning-choice seed example in the authoring prompt (it propagated, including a duplicate slides-vs-walk in CH23 and CH25). Cap at ~3 chapters; ban the 'has N minutes before X / blank calendar / budgets the minutes / no execution yet' frame and the 'three named slots' divide. Immediately rewrite CH23 OR CH25 so the slides-vs-walk choice appears only once.

families.name: phone-away remedy / 'put the phone in another room, facedown'
families.signature: The single recycled actionable tactic — put the phone in another room/hall, set it facedown, charge it outside the bedroom, set shoes by the door — reused as the marquee TRY-NOW / HOOK / ifThen / example move across at least seven chapters spanning different domains.
exemplarQuotes: CH7 TRY-NOW: 'put your phone in another room'
CH25 HOOK: 'shoes by the door and the phone facedown' + TRY-NOW 'Set your walking shoes beside the door'
CH28 ex3: 'Phone is in the hall' + TRY-NOW 'put your phone in another room and place one blank page'
CH30 ex6: 'puts the phone face down' + TRY-NOW 'move your phone charger outside the bedroom'
families.fix: Build a per-domain TRY-NOW tactic palette so each chapter's marquee action is distinct (e.g., breath count, one-sentence note, a single closed tab, a walk, a named object) and allow the phone-away remedy in at most 2 chapters book-wide. Coordinate with the routine-reset family so 'phone face down' is not also the recurring example gesture.

families.name: kitchen-table stamp + templated TRY-NOW opener
families.signature: The 'kitchen table' is the default scene venue (14 of 34 chapters) AND the venue baked into a near-verbatim templated TRY-NOW: 'Put/Make a [N]-minute [check/reset/block] on tomorrow's calendar for [8:1x a.m.] at your kitchen table, triggered by [first inbox/criticism/quiet block].'
exemplarQuotes: CH5 TRY-NOW: 'Make tomorrow at 9:10 a.m. a 15-minute question review at your kitchen table'
CH11 TRY-NOW: 'Put a 12-minute service check on tomorrow's calendar for 8:20 at your kitchen table'
CH26 TRY-NOW: 'Put a 12-minute reset on tomorrow's calendar for 8:15 a.m. at your kitchen table'
CH32 TRY-NOW: 'Put a 12-minute Aftermath Check on tomorrow's calendar for 8:30 p.m. at your kitchen table'
families.fix: Diversify scene venues (limit 'kitchen table' to ~3 chapters) and de-template the TRY-NOW: drop the fixed 'on tomorrow's calendar at your kitchen table' formula and the 8:1x morning time band; let each chapter pick a place, time, and trigger native to its lesson. Treat the TRY-NOW opener as a banned exact phrase in the gate.

families.name: generic-room venues (conference room / break room)
families.signature: Structurally similar review/coaching/hot-reply beats keep landing in low-distinctiveness corporate rooms — 'conference room / conference room table' (twice with identical 'empty conference room' framing) and 'break room' — compounding the same-setting feel alongside the kitchen-table stamp.
exemplarQuotes: CH8: 'Sharon tells Constance in the empty conference room' / domain='conference room coaching'
CH17 HOOK: 'The conference room was empty except for a closed laptop and Anne Frank's chestnut tree on the screen'
CH2: 'he sits in the break room for five minutes, remembers Blaise Pascal in 1654 France'
CH20: 'Hailey sends her version from the break room before the coffee cools'
families.fix: Add a setting-variety constraint across the book so example venues draw from a wide pool (clinic, kitchen, bakery, classroom, transit, outdoors, home) rather than clustering into kitchen-table/conference-room/break-room. Ban the repeated 'empty conference room' framing; assign distinct venues per chapter at plan time.

families.name: Tiger-Woods 2009-scandal exemplar reuse
families.signature: The Tiger Woods / 2009 scandal / PGA Tour 'public mastery beside private disorder' case used as a full teaching unit in three chapters with the same framing — visible skill does not govern private appetite.
exemplarQuotes: CH9 FAST-READ: 'The same career later met the 2009 scandal.'
CH14 card: 'Tiger Woods and Earl Woods show that public skill can grow beside private pressure.'
CH15 ex1: 'a note comparing the pattern to Tiger Woods's 2009 public scandal' / FAST-READ 'After 2009, Tiger Woods was not a puzzle because he lacked discipline.'
families.fix: Assign Tiger Woods to a single chapter and give CH9/CH14/CH15 distinct exemplars from a shared source registry that enforces one-figure-one-chapter. Maintain a cross-chapter case ledger so no celebrity case anchors more than one chapter.

families.name: Dorothy-Day / Catholic-Worker exemplar reuse
families.signature: The Dorothy Day / Catholic Worker / New York Great Depression soup-line case recurs across three chapters, each tying 'calm/inner life must become outward service,' with the same soup line, beds, and 1933 stamping.
exemplarQuotes: CH12 ex1: 'Lionel wipes tomato soup... before the Catholic Worker supper in New York City. Dorothy Day had stronger nerves than I do'
CH13 FAST-READ: 'Dorothy Day's kind of stillness... became bread, beds, letters'
CH33 ex2: 'A Catholic Worker newsletter... folded open to Dorothy Day, pacifism, and arrests'
families.fix: Pin Dorothy Day / Catholic Worker to one chapter via the source registry; re-source the others. Enforce one-figure-one-chapter and flag repeated proper-noun stamping (New York, Great Depression, 1933) in the gate.

families.name: Fred-Rogers / 1968-Pittsburgh exemplar reuse
families.signature: Fred Rogers / 1968 Pittsburgh / Mister Rogers' Neighborhood anchors three chapters; CH12 and CH19 repeat the same '1968 ... studio ... spoke to children ... slowly' beat almost verbatim, CH26 reuses the figure for routine (143 pounds / daily swim).
exemplarQuotes: CH12 FAST-READ: 'Fred Rogers sat in a 1968 PBS studio'
CH19 FAST-READ: 'The 1968 Pittsburgh host sat in a studio and spoke to children'
CH26 FAST-READ: 'Fred Rogers kept a daily swim in Pittsburgh and weighed himself at 143 pounds'
families.fix: Assign Fred Rogers to one chapter only; re-source CH12/CH19/CH26 from the registry. Ban repeated '1968 Pittsburgh studio / spoke to children slowly' phrasing across chapters.

families.name: Marcus-Aurelius / Meditations framing-source reuse
families.signature: Marcus Aurelius / Meditations / Roman Empire / second century reused as the framing source in three non-adjacent chapters, each with the 'ruler with the empire on his back still wrote private notes' beat and 'second century' stamping.
exemplarQuotes: CH6 FAST-READ: 'Marcus Aurelius had the Roman Empire on his back'
CH13 DEEP-READ: 'In Meditations, Marcus Aurelius keeps calling himself back to work. The Roman Empire did not wait for his mood.'
CH34 card: 'Marcus Aurelius used death as a guide for conduct in the second century'
families.fix: Limit Marcus Aurelius / Meditations to one anchoring chapter; allow a brief callback elsewhere only if it does not re-stamp 'Roman Empire / second century / empire on his back.' Track marquee-text usage in the source registry.

families.name: Stoic-under-Nero/Nicopolis framing reuse
families.signature: The 'Stoic philosopher working under pressure in Rome near Nero / Nicopolis' unit (Seneca in CH4 and CH11, Epictetus in CH22) repeats the same beat — a Stoic stayed clear-minded amid danger/noise, therefore so can you — with CH4 and CH11 both stamping 'Rome ... Nero.'
exemplarQuotes: CH4 ex2: 'Lucius Annaeus Seneca working in noisy Rome under Nero'
CH11 FAST-READ: 'Seneca in Rome, steady enough to think near Nero'
CH22 FAST-READ: 'Epictetus did not ask students in Nicopolis'
families.fix: Treat 'Stoic-stayed-calm-under-Nero/Nicopolis' as one occupied slot; use Seneca-near-Nero in at most one chapter and re-source the others (different tradition or figure). Add the 'Rome ... Nero' stamp to the gate's repeated-phrase watchlist.

families.name: Anne-Frank / Secret-Annex exemplar reuse
families.signature: Anne Frank's 1942 Amsterdam diary / Secret Annex is the emotional centerpiece in two chapters (diary for private writing in CH6; chestnut tree for beauty in CH17), with the same Amsterdam / Secret Annex stamping.
exemplarQuotes: CH6 ex2: 'After reading Anne Frank's 1942 diary from Amsterdam' / card 'Anne Frank's diary held fear, longing, humor, and ordinary detail'
CH17 ex1: 'Anne Frank's chestnut tree from the Secret Annex in Amsterdam' / card 'The chestnut tree did not remove danger from the Secret Annex'
families.fix: Assign Anne Frank to one chapter; re-source the other from the registry. One-figure-one-chapter enforcement applies even when the two uses pull different facets (diary vs chestnut tree).

families.name: Kennedy / Cuban-Missile-Crisis exemplar reuse
families.signature: The Kennedy / Cuban Missile Crisis / October 1962 case anchors both Become Present and Act Bravely with the same 'maps in the room, advisers wanted the loud strike, he slowed it' beat and identical October-1962 stamping.
exemplarQuotes: CH2 FAST-READ: 'In October 1962, John F. Kennedy sat with maps of Cuba, reports on Soviet missiles, and a room pulled toward military speed.'
CH33 FAST-READ: 'Strike maps still sat in the room after John F. Kennedy chose a naval quarantine in October 1962. Some advisers wanted air strikes. The braver move was not the loud one.'
families.fix: Pin Kennedy / October 1962 to one chapter; re-source the other. Flag the shared 'maps in the room / advisers wanted air strikes / October 1962' beat in the gate's repeated-exemplar check.

families.name: control-distinction column exercise + 'supervise the sky' line
families.signature: The Stoic 'control distinction' column-sorting exercise (mine / not mine; accept / change / ask) is the core mechanic of both Let Go and Accept a Higher Power, and both close on the same 'stop supervising the universe / whole sky' image — effectively one reused unit split across two chapters.
exemplarQuotes: CH10 ex2: 'he writes two columns on a yellow pad: mine, not mine' + MEMORABLE 'The energy that was going into supervision of the universe returns to the work in front of him.'
CH18 DEEP-READ: 'Tamar draws three lines: accept... change... ask wisdom' + MEMORABLE 'Stillness grows where the self no longer has to supervise the whole sky.'
families.fix: Differentiate the two chapters: keep the column-sorting artifact in one and give the other a distinct mechanic. Ban the 'supervise the universe / whole sky' MEMORABLE line from appearing in more than one chapter.

families.name: old-threat ifThen / 'mild comment lands like shame/attack'
families.signature: Adjacent chapters open their plan ifThen list with the same trigger ('a mild comment lands like shame/an attack') and the same remedy ('write the old meaning/exact sentence before you answer'); CH14's quiz-opener restates it again.
exemplarQuotes: CH12 ifThen: '[A mild comment lands in your body like shame.] -> ... run the Soul Alignment Check and write the old meaning before you answer the present person.'
CH14 ifThen: '[A mild comment lands like an attack.] -> ... Name the Old Threat by writing the exact sentence and the older meaning before you answer.'
families.fix: Rewrite one chapter's lead ifThen trigger and remedy so the 'mild comment feels like shame/attack -> write the old meaning before you answer' branch appears once. Coordinate ifThen triggers across adjacent chapters at plan time to avoid duplicate lead branches.

families.name: input-discipline spaced-recall callback boilerplate
families.signature: The 'Earlier concept: Limit Your Inputs / input discipline' spaced-recall card recurs as a near-boilerplate callback in many later chapters, each re-summarizing input discipline in uniform wording.
exemplarQuotes: CH9: 'Input discipline limits the applause, outrage, gossip'
CH24 card: 'Earlier concept, Limit Your Inputs'
CH30 card: 'Earlier concept: how does input discipline support the bedtime line?'
CH33 card: 'Earlier concept, Limit Your Inputs: how does less noise prepare quiet courage?'
families.fix: Vary which earlier concept each spaced-recall card calls back to (rotate across the full concept set) so 'Limit Your Inputs' is not the default callback, and vary the recap phrasing. Low severity but cheap: enforce callback-target diversity at plan time.

families.name: recycled first-name collision (Benjamin, Pascal)
families.signature: A first name carries a famous source figure in one chapter and an unrelated fictional present-day protagonist in a nearby chapter: 'Benjamin' = Benjamin Franklin (CH26) vs a modern consultant (CH29); 'Pascal' = Blaise Pascal (CH2) vs a modern training supervisor (CH30).
exemplarQuotes: CH26: 'The model is Benjamin Franklin's morning question and evening review' vs CH29: 'Benjamin writes the memo at 6:12 p.m.: Decision before Friday dinner...'
CH30: 'Pascal expects the training score to jump after Madeline adds a 9 p.m. study block' vs CH2: 'Felix tries Pascal's quiet room test... remembers Blaise Pascal in 1654 France'
families.fix: Add every historical figure's first name to the protagonist-name exclusion pool so fictional protagonists never reuse a source figure's first name. Rename the CH29 and CH30 protagonists (currently Benjamin and Pascal) to non-colliding names.

families: records-audit / 'nothing dramatic happens, the telling detail'
before/after diptych / 'same object, one variable flips'
planning-choice / 'N minutes before X, nothing started yet'
records-audit / 'nothing dramatic happens, the telling detail'

synthesis.summary: The book is built from a small fixed set of pedagogy-slot scene machines and a tiny pool of exemplars/venues, so it reads as one template re-skinned 34 times rather than 34 distinct chapters. Nine scene-skeleton families (postmortem-autopsy, mistake-recovery 'halfway through, hears themselves', records-audit 'nothing dramatic happens / the telling detail', two-person 'same X, two minds' contrast, routine break/stop/restart, Before:/After: diptych, timestamped 'Subject:' decision-memo, and 'N minutes before X' planning-choice) each recur in 13-18 chapters with near-verbatim framing phrases and payoff lines; two of them (records-audit and planning-choice) are literally the authoring prompt's own seed examples reproduced downstream, and CH23/CH25 even duplicate the same slides-vs-walk choice almost line-for-line. On top of the structural reuse, a handful of historical exemplars (Tiger Woods, Dorothy Day, Fred Rogers, Marcus Aurelius, Seneca/Epictetus-under-Nero, Anne Frank, Kennedy/Cuban Missile Crisis) each anchor 2-3 chapters with identical date/place stamping, the marquee actionable tactic collapses to 'put the phone facedown/in another room' across seven chapters, the scene venue collapses to 'kitchen table' in 14 of 34 chapters (plus a templated 'on tomorrow's calendar at your kitchen table' TRY-NOW), and source-figure first names (Benjamin, Pascal) collide with fictional protagonists. The single highest-leverage fix is to stop the templates at the source: strip the records-audit and planning-choice seed examples out of the authoring prompt and impose a per-book quota system — each scene-skeleton format capped at ~3 chapters, each historical figure/case used in exactly one chapter, each chapter drawing a distinct TRY-NOW tactic and venue from rotating palettes, all enforced by a cross-chapter banned-phrase + one-figure-one-chapter gate so no frame, payoff line, exemplar, or venue can repeat book-wide.
